title: Foundational principles
line: Independent, deterministic tests at the right level of the pyramid, with fast feedback.
points: Each test sets up its own state and can run alone, in any order and in parallel.
The same input gives the same result. Flakiness is a defect, not noise.
Push checks down to unit, API and contract tests. Keep UI end-to-end tests thin and focused on critical journeys.
Short suites on every commit, broader suites nightly, with smoke and regression tiers.
Tests are production-grade code: review, naming conventions, DRY, SOLID and linting all apply.
One behavior per test, with failure messages that point to the cause.
Test early in the pipeline, and verify in production with synthetic monitoring.

title: Architecture & design patterns
line: Layered suites: specs, domain actions, page or API objects, drivers. No locators in specs.
points: Separate specs, domain actions, page or API abstractions, and low-level drivers or clients.
Page and component objects encapsulate UI structure; component objects scale better than one giant page class.
Screenplay describes tests as actors performing tasks and asking questions.
API client wrappers give one place for HTTP or SDK interaction, with typed models.
Factories and builders create test data with sensible defaults and per-test overrides.
Inject drivers, clients and config instead of using singletons or static globals.
Strategies swap browsers, devices, environments or auth methods without changing tests.
BDD (Gherkin) is only worth it if business stakeholders actually read the specs.

title: Isolation & context
line: Every test gets its own context, data and typed state store, cleaned up automatically.
points: Every test gets its own browser context or session, HTTP client, cookies, storage and user account.
Use thread-local, async-local or per-worker containers, never mutable statics.
Pass data between steps through a typed, test-scoped context object, not a stringly-typed map.
Clean up in teardown even on failure; better still, use unique data so cleanup isn't needed for correctness.

title: Parallelism & scale
line: Worker-scoped resources, sharding by duration and ephemeral environments.
points: Run in parallel at file, test or scenario level, with worker-scoped resources.
Shard across CI machines, ideally balanced by historical duration.
Give parallel runs unique names, IDs or tenants, and lease dedicated accounts from a pool.
Use containers or per-PR environments so tests never fight over shared state.
Drive cross-browser and device matrices from config, not code.

title: Synchronization
line: Never sleep. Wait on signals, with web-first assertions and layered timeouts.
points: Never use fixed sleeps.
Wait for an element state, network response, event or DOM condition.
Use web-first assertions that poll until a timeout.
Wait on signals, not time: a specific API response or a job status polled with backoff and a hard timeout.
Treat timeouts as layered configuration, tuned per environment.
For async backends, poll for eventual consistency instead of asserting immediately.

title: Reliability & flakes
line: Retry at the right level, quarantine with an owner and capture traces on failure.
points: Retry known transient actions; allow one or two test-level retries as a CI safety net, not a fix.
Never retry assertions on real business outcomes just to make them pass.
Track pass rates per test, tag flaky tests and quarantine them with an owner and a deadline.
Capture traces, videos, screenshots, HAR files and logs on failure.
Prefer dedicated test IDs, then role or accessibility locators, over brittle XPath and CSS chains.
Treat self-healing locators as suggestions; they can mask real regressions.

title: Test data
line: API-driven setup, builders with overrides and seeded synthetic data.
points: Drive tests from tables, CSV, JSON or generators.
Create preconditions through APIs or the database, not the UI.
Use synthetic data generators with seeded randomness so failures reproduce.
Keep golden datasets for read-only reference data, with clear lifecycle rules.
Keep secrets in a vault or CI secrets, never in the repo.
Layer configuration (defaults, environment, local override) with no environment values in test code.

title: Test doubles
line: Mocks, network interception, contract tests and control over clocks and flags.
points: Mock, stub or virtualize third-party and unstable dependencies.
Intercept the network to simulate failures, latency and edge cases deterministically.
Use contract testing to decouple service tests from full end-to-end environments.
Control clocks and feature flags so tests are deterministic.

title: Assertions
line: Expressive failures, schema validation and non-functional checks in one framework.
points: Write expressive assertions with rich failure output.
Use soft assertions to gather several failures in one run.
Validate API responses against schemas and contracts.
Run accessibility, visual, performance-budget and basic security checks in the same framework.

title: Observability & CI/CD
line: Correlated logs, rich reports, quality gates and test impact analysis.
points: Use structured logs with correlation IDs that link test steps to backend traces.
Publish rich reports with step detail, attachments, history and trends.
Run headless and containerized, cache dependencies and keep artifacts on failure.
Gate merges and deployments on tests, with tags to select suites.
Run only the tests affected by a change.
Track duration, flake rate, critical-path coverage and time to diagnose failures.

title: Maintainability
line: Conventions, composable helpers, regular pruning and clear ownership.
points: Agree on naming, folder layout and tagging, and document how to write a test.
Prefer small, composable helpers over deep inheritance.
Delete redundant or low-value tests regularly.
Give every test area an owner and triage failures fast.
Pin tool, browser and driver versions and run in containers.
